questions.q: In the primary deformities of CTEV, 'A' stands for Adduction, occurring at the:
questions.exp: A: adduction at talonavicular / mid tarsal joint. (Book p169)

questions.q: In the primary deformities of CTEV, 'V' stands for Varus, occurring at the:
questions.exp: V: varus at talocalcaneal / subtalar joint. (Book p169)

questions.q: In the primary deformities of CTEV, 'E' stands for Equinus, occurring at the:
questions.exp: E: equinus at ankle joint. (Book p169)

questions.q: Besides the CAVE deformities, CTEV also shows:
questions.exp: Internal rotation of tibia is also seen in CTEV. (Book p169)

questions.q: The screening test for CTEV is the:
questions.exp: Screening test: dorsiflexion test. (Book p169)

questions.q: In the dorsiflexion test, a NORMAL foot:
opts: Has the dorsum of the foot usually touching the shin
questions.exp: Normal: dorsum of the foot usually touches the shin (passive dorsiflexion possible). (Book p169)

questions.q: In the dorsiflexion test, a CLUB FOOT:
opts: Dorsiflexion is not possible even on strong pressure
questions.exp: Club foot: dorsiflexion is not possible even on strong pressure. (Book p169)

questions.q: The confirmatory test / angle for CTEV is Kite's angle, which is the:
questions.exp: Confirmatory test: Kite's angle: talocalcaneal angle. (Book p169)

questions.q: The normal Kite's angle is:
questions.exp: Normal Kite's angle: 30-40 degree; in CTEV the angle between talus and calcaneum becomes zero (parallel). (Book p169)

questions.q: Treatment of CTEV in the newborn should be started:
questions.exp: Treatment in newborn: start treatment by 2 weeks. (Book p170)

questions.q: In the Ponseti method, the order of manipulation is:
questions.exp: Order of manipulation: Ponseti method: C -> V and A -> E. (Book p170)

questions.q: In the Ponseti method, after each manipulation the deformity is maintained with POP:
opts: Above the knee, kept for 1 week, procedure repeated after 1 week (7-8 weeks)
At the ankle only, for 1 month
questions.exp: Manipulation of foot -> maintain with POP (7-8 weeks), above the knee, keep for 1 week, repeat procedure after 1 week. (Book p170)

questions.q: Treatment in Ponseti's method starts at:
questions.exp: Ponseti's method: treatment starts <2 weeks; Kite's method: 1 month. (Book p170)

questions.q: In Kite's method, the order of correction is:
questions.exp: Kite's method order: adduction -> inversion -> equinus. (Book p170)

questions.q: The fulcrum in Ponseti's method is the:
questions.exp: Fulcrum: Ponseti's method: head of talus; Kite's method: calcaneocuboid joint. (Book p170)

questions.q: The POP type used in Ponseti's method is the:
questions.exp: POP type: Ponseti's method: above knee cast; Kite's method: below knee cast. (Book p170)

questions.q: The duration of treatment in Ponseti's method is:
questions.exp: Duration: Ponseti's method: 6-8 weeks; Kite's method: 6-9 months. (Book p170)

questions.q: Rocker bottom foot is caused by:
opts: Overcorrection of CTEV and congenital vertical talus
questions.exp: Rocker bottom foot causes: overcorrection of CTEV; congenital vertical talus. (Book p170)

questions.q: The Dennis Brown splint is used in CTEV:
opts: Till the baby learns to walk; as the baby moves the leg the deformity keeps getting corrected; disadvantage: low compliance
questions.exp: Prevention of recurrence: Dennis Brown splint till the baby learns to walk; mechanism: as baby moves the leg, deformity keeps getting corrected; disadvantage: low compliance. (Book p170)

questions.q: CTEV shoes are worn:
opts: Once the baby starts walking, up to the age of 3-5 yrs; Dennis Brown splint when the baby sleeps; at least 23 hrs/day
questions.exp: CTEV shoes: once the baby starts walking (up to age 3-5 yrs); use Dennis Brown splint when baby sleeps; should be worn at least 23 hrs/day. (Book p170)

questions.q: The design features of CTEV shoes include all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: A high medial heel (to force inversion)
questions.exp: CTEV shoes: straight inner border -> to prevent adduction; outer raise -> prevents varus; absence of heel -> prevents equinus. (Book p170)

questions.q: Treatment of CTEV at 1-3 years is:
opts: Posteromedial soft tissue release with/without Ponseti manipulation
questions.exp: 1-3 yrs: posteromedial soft tissue release +/w Ponseti manipulation (soft tissues contract by 1 year of age). (Book p170)

questions.q: Turco's procedure releases the following soft tissues:
opts: Tendoachilles, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus
questions.exp: Turco's procedure: to release the soft tissue (tendoachilles, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus). (Book p170)

questions.q: In CTEV at 3-5 years:
opts: By 3 yrs forefoot adduction becomes bony - AMSTR + Dilwyn Evans' procedure
questions.exp: 3-5 yrs: by 3 yrs forefoot adduction becomes bony; AMSTR + Dilwyn Evans' procedure. (Book p171)

questions.q: Dilwyn Evans' procedure is:
opts: Lateral column shortening by calcaneocuboid fusion
questions.exp: Dilwyn Evans' procedure: lateral column shortening by calcaneocuboid fusion. (Book p171)

questions.q: In CTEV at 5-8 years:
opts: By 5 years varus becomes bony - Dilwyn's Evans + Dwyer's osteotomy (wedge osteotomy)
questions.exp: 5-8 yrs: by 5 years varus becomes bony; Dilwyn's Evans + Dwyer's osteotomy (wedge osteotomy). (Book p171)

questions.q: The treatment of CTEV at 6-10 years is:
questions.exp: 6-10 yrs: wedge tarsectomy. (Book p171)

questions.q: In CTEV beyond 10 years, the treatment is triple arthrodesis - surgical fusion of:
questions.exp: Triple arthrodesis: surgical fusion of talonavicular, talocalcaneal and calcaneocuboid joint. (Book p171)

questions.q: The complication of triple arthrodesis if performed below 10 yrs of age is:
questions.exp: Complication: if performed below 10 yrs of age -> arthrodesis fails -> pseudoarthrosis. (Book p171)

questions.q: The deformity correction device for CTEV is Josh's external stabilization system, based on:
questions.exp: Deformity correction device: Josh's external stabilization system; based on Ilizarov's principle of external fixation. (Book p171)

questions.q: Achondroplasia is the m/c cause of:
questions.exp: Achondroplasia: m/c cause of disproportionate dwarfism. (Book p172)

questions.q: The etiology of achondroplasia is:
questions.exp: Etiology: FGFR3 gene mutation on chromosome 4. (Book p172)

questions.q: The inheritance of achondroplasia is:
questions.exp: Autosomal dominant inheritance or sporadic. (Book p172)

questions.q: The pathogenesis of achondroplasia is:
opts: Affects endochondral ossification of long bones; intramembranous ossification is normal (flat bones of skull and clavicle)
Affects cartilage only in the hands
questions.exp: Pathogenesis: affects endochondral ossification of long bones; intramembranous ossification is normal (flat bones of skull and clavicle). (Book p172)

questions.q: The limb shortening in achondroplasia is:
questions.exp: Clinical features: proximal limb shortening (rhizomelic shortening). (Book p172)

questions.q: In achondroplasia, the trunk is:
questions.exp: Trunk is usually normal. (Book p172)

questions.q: Patients with achondroplasia have:
questions.exp: Patients have normal IQ and sexual development. (Book p172)

questions.q: Brachydactyly in achondroplasia means:
questions.exp: Brachydactyly: short, stubby fingers. (Book p172)

questions.q: The skull feature in achondroplasia is:
questions.exp: Frontal bossing of skull. (Book p172)

questions.q: The hand findings in achondroplasia include:
questions.exp: Hand features: starfish hand; trident hand. (Book p172)

questions.q: The vertebral finding in achondroplasia is:
questions.exp: Bullet nose vertebrae. (Book p172)

questions.q: The pelvic finding in achondroplasia is the:
questions.exp: Champagne glass pelvis. (Book p172)

questions.q: Another facial feature of achondroplasia is:
questions.exp: Saddle nose. (Book p172)

questions.q: Shortening of the middle part of the limb is called:
questions.exp: Note: shortening of middle part of limb: mesomelic. (Book p172)

questions.q: Shortening of the distal part of the limb is called:
questions.exp: Note: shortening of distal part of limb: acromelic. (Book p172)

units.title: Deformities of the Knee
units.guide: Four shapes define the bowed child: genu varum bowing away from the midline, genu valgum knocking towards it, the windswept twist of one varus and one valgus leg, and genu recurvatum's excessive backward bend. In children rickets tops the list for varum and windswept while idiopathy wins for valgum; in adults osteoarthritis drives varum, rheumatoid arthritis drives valgum and windswept.

units.title: Blount's Disease
units.guide: Blount's disease - infantile tibia vara - is bilateral idiopathic genu varum built on a proximal medial tibial physis defect, adding internal tibial rotation and genu recurvatum. Sifert Katz sign marks the clinic; metaphyseal beaking marks the film.

units.title: Knee: Causes & Osteotomy
units.guide: Acquired knee deformity follows malunion or growth plate injury, and the osteotomist corrects with wedges: open wedge lengthens the short side by filling extra bone, closed wedge shortens the long side by removing bone.

units.title: Anatomy of the Foot
units.guide: Three joints move the foot: the tibio-talar (ankle) plantar- and dorsiflexes, the subtalar inverts and everts, and the talonavicular with calcaneocuboid (mid tarsal) joints adduct and abduct the forefoot. The medial longitudinal arch gives the foot its concavity - lose it and it is flat, exaggerate it and it is cavus.

units.title: Deformity & Talipes Terminology
units.guide: Ankle plantarflexion is equinus, dorsiflexion is calcaneus; subtalar inversion is varus, eversion is valgus. Talipes - the congenitally twisted foot - then names the combinations: cavus (high arch), equinus (plantarflexed), calcaneus (dorsiflexed), valgus (abducted, everted) and varus (adducted, inverted).

units.title: CTEV: Introduction
units.guide: Club foot - CTEV, the m/c congenital abnormality of leg, ankle and foot, appearing like a golf club. One in 1000 live births, half bilateral, boys over girls, first born with breech presentation. The m/c form is congenital/primary and m/c idiopathic, but watch for spina bifida and arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (muscle fibrosis to contracture to deformity); acquired club foot belongs to neuromuscular disorders like poliomyelitis.

units.title: CTEV: Pathoanatomy
units.guide: A hypoplastic small talus displaces at the talonavicular joint, the foot destabilizes, and the Achilles and tibialis posterior pull it back and medially: talus in equinus and varus, calcaneus inverted, forefoot varus, ankle plantarflexed. The CAVE acronym maps it: Cavus (exaggerated medial arch), Adduction (talonavicular/mid tarsal), Varus (subtalar), Equinus (ankle) - with internal tibial rotation along for the ride.

units.title: CTEV: Tests
units.guide: Screen with the dorsiflexion test: the normal foot's dorsum touches the shin, the club foot will not dorsiflex even under strong pressure. Confirm with Kite's angle - the talocalcaneal angle, normally 30-40 degrees, collapsing to zero (parallel talus and calcaneum) in CTEV.

units.title: CTEV: Newborn Treatment
units.guide: Start by 2 weeks and work Ponseti's order - Cavus, then Varus and Adduction, then Equinus - each manipulation held in an above-knee POP for a week, six to eight weeks overall, pivoting on the head of the talus. Kite's rival method starts at 1 month, corrects adduction-inversion then equinus on the calcaneocuboid fulcrum, below-knee casting for 6-9 months. Overcorrect and you make a rocker bottom foot, as does congenital vertical talus.

units.title: CTEV: Preventing Recurrence
units.guide: Recurrence is the enemy: the Dennis Brown splint works till the baby walks (and suffers low compliance), then CTEV shoes take over up to 3-5 years - worn at least 23 hours a day with the splint at sleep. The shoe is engineered against relapse: straight inner border against adduction, outer raise against varus, absent heel against equinus.

units.title: CTEV: Late Presentation
units.guide: The late club foot stiffens with age and the surgery follows the clock: 1-3 years posteromedial soft tissue release with or without Ponseti manipulation (Turco releases the Achilles, tibialis posterior and FDL); 3-5 years, forefoot adduction turned bony, gets AMSTR plus Dilwyn Evans' calcaneocuboid fusion; 5-8 years, varus turned bony, adds Dwyer's wedge osteotomy; 6-10 years wedge tarsectomy; and beyond 10, triple arthrodesis fusing talonavicular, talocalcaneal and calcaneocuboid - which done before 10 fails to pseudoarthrosis. Josh's external stabilization system, on Ilizarov's principle, stands ready for deformity correction.

units.title: Achondroplasia
units.guide: Achondroplasia, the m/c disproportionate dwarfism, is an FGFR3 mutation on chromosome 4 - autosomal dominant or sporadic - that blocks endochondral but not intramembranous ossification. Rhizomelic shortening with a normal trunk, normal IQ and sexual development; the face gives frontal bossing and saddle nose, the hands a starfish or trident span, the spine bullet-nose vertebrae, the pelvis a champagne glass. Shortening terminology: middle limb mesomelic, distal acromelic.
